EDITORIAL NOTE OR EDITORIAL GREDOS, S. A. Sánchez Pacheco, 85, Madrid, 1998.

Some years ago, Editorial Gredos commissioned the translation of the Letters of Cipriano of Cartago to Professor José María Romeo Pallás, who shortly afterwards expressed his desire to share this work with his student Dr." García Sanchidrián. Unfortunately, after the death of Professor Romeo in April 1994, it was not possible to find the part of the translation that he had already done, so the entirety of it had to be entrusted to Professor García Sanchidrián. Therefore, this note serves as clarification and, above all, as a posthumous and emotional memory of Professor Romeo. José Javier Iso Echegoyen September 1998

1. Historical setting

For thirty years, Christianity also discredited the peace that the Roman government granted to the Jewish people, not because freedom had been granted consciously, but because neither the government nor the people distinguished between Christianity and Judaism. At first the adepts continued to observe Jewish law in Jerusalem; but the Church, according to the Acts of the Apostles, increased rapidly, as many Jews who visited Jerusalem for Easter converted to Christianity. Being persecuted by the Jews, the Christian leaders were immediately driven from Jerusalem to the synagogues of Samaria and Syria, where they were followed by several of their persecutors, including Saul. Soon the Gospel would be preached to the Gentiles, and the converts would be free to abandon the practice of Judaism. The apostle of the Gentiles could now preach a Gospel emancipated from Judaism2, although the hostility of the ((Judaizers)) hindered all his steps.

Paul traveled along the roads of commerce and communications to which the Roman peace had given security. He first visited the Jewish communities and then preached to the Gentiles3, in the Greek of that time. His converts generally belonged to the humble classes4. When his preaching promoted disorders, it was the Jews who provoked them5. Roman officials protected him as a Jewish sectarian. But, if at that time the government of Rome did not distinguish between Judaism and Christianity, the people did not take long to do so, because they understood that something more insolent and something more dangerous than Judaism had emerged. Around the year 64 AD. C., the date of Nero's persecution7, the government had finally realized this, since, according to its enemies, Christianity deserved to be given official surveillance, because it did not satisfy the conditions under which Rome granted tolerance8. This captivity lasted two years (58-60) in the Caesarea prison, because Felix, although convinced of his innocence, did not dare to become angry with the Jews. For this reason Paul enjoyed relative freedom. But as the proconsul Festus, Felix's successor, insisted that he should be tried by the Sanhedrin, Paul appealed to Caesar, for which he was sent to Rome. On the coast of Italy the Christians of Puzzuoli received him with great displays of affection (Acts 28, 13); Then he was taken to Rome, where Christians came out to meet him. He was held there, in prison, for two years with the sole supervision of a soldier, thus being able to maintain frequent contact with Christians and continue his apostolate with others. G. To some Romans of the time it seemed that Christians hated the human race; They looked forward to the coming advent of Christ when all but themselves would be destroyed. From the 11th century onwards this way of thinking manifested itself in a different way; Christians did not mind provoking enmity in order to win the crown of martyrdom. By refusing to cooperate in religious festivals, amphitheater games, theater shows and circuses, to manifest the gestures of worship that permeated ordinary life, they called into question the legislation and institutions of the city. They defended values ​​that were not identified with the Roman Empire. The message of Christians is vaster and more lasting than empires and civilizations, which are built and destroyed: this attitude will be described as indifference and lack of civility, because the official religion is one with the city. So one side thought in political terms, the other in religious terms; and, since the Christian religion was absolutely different from all others in its rejection of the slogan "live and let live", the conflict was inevitable. Since the first persecution, that is, that of Nero, carrying the "name" of Christian, which was equivalent to being complicit in subversive practices, was enough to be persecuted. On the other hand, it seems that in the first two centuries there was no "general" edict against Christianity. The persecution was sporadic and local. It is produced

If it is proven that someone is a Christian, they must be punished. Anonymous complaints should not be taken into consideration 12. It seems that Trajan, despite the large number of Christians that according to Pliny there were in Bithynia, did not consider them to be actively dangerous. During the reigns of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, persecution was generally initiated by the fury of the populace rather than by official initiative 13. In the 111th and 4th centuries the relationship between Church and State underwent changes that were linked to the changes in circumstances that both had experienced. The persecution was now carried out by general edict of the Emperor and not by the local exercise of judicial initiative. Furthermore, Christianity had defined itself both in its external organization and in its doctrine in relation to the problems of human life in the Empire. It was already the religion of some of the most competent and cultured men of the time. But at this time what mattered most desperately to the State was unity. This new phase is characterized as an open and general battle against Christianity, with the aim of destroying it, believing it to be a danger to the State. The change that occurred in the relationship between Christianity and the government is seen more clearly by examining the reasons that caused the persecution. Septimius Severus was not hostile at first, and is known to have given his son Caracalla to the care of a Christian nurse, as Tertullian writes in his Apologeticum, 16 15. But he was alarmed by the rapid increase in the number of Christians and forbade the baptism of pagans, although this prohibition expired after his death. The measures of Decius, a man of great qualities as a warrior and ruler, were more drastic, and motivated by the increasingly numerous indications that the l4 Apologetic 37.

Despite the improvement in the situation of Christians in the reign of Septimius Severus, persecution continued in Africa, due to the proconsul Scapula. TERTULIAN speaks at length about her, in Ad Scapulam 4, which also states that Caracalla was lacte christiano educatus. There are some records of martyrs from this time, but they have little value.

The Church was being organized as an exclusive section of society, because of its pacifism and the consequent threat to the military effectiveness of the Empire, and because of the Emperor's desire to maintain good relations with the Senate. For all this, Decius judged Christianity, already very developed, an obstacle to his plans, which is why he ordered, by means of a general edict against them 16, that all citizens appear before the magistrate, make sacrifices to the pagan gods and receive a certificate accrediting having made them. For a short time there was fierce persecution, originally intended to cause mass renouncement of the faith. The edict was successful because, although there were many martyrs, there were also many lapses, due to fear of the new method and also, according to Cyprian (De lapsis 5, 6), due to the laxity of many Christians. But the imperial purposes failed because almost every time, some even during the persecution itself, they asked to be admitted back into the Church. Their admission to the Church provoked disputes, the so-called controversy of the lapses, about penitential discipline and its dogmatic foundations on the occasion of that conflict: we will talk about it later. In the year 257 AD. C., Valerian tried to impose the tolerance of Christianity, which had been denied for two centuries, ordering that the high clergy make sacrifices, but allowing them to continue being Christian in private life 17. In the year 257 he published an edict against the clerics and shortly after another against all Christians, apparently alleging political danger. But it was under Diocletian that the bloodiest persecution broke out. The emperor had set out to give Rome extraordinary splendor. In his desperate effort to unite the Empire, he was especially concerned about influences that tended toward separatism, and, although he initially despised the strength of the Christians, by 303 AD. C., under pressure from Caesar Galerius, his associate in the government, he had come to the conclusion that there was indeed another State within the State. The measures he took were unprecedented, since no Christian could enjoy Roman citizenship or, therefore, hold positions in the imperial or municipal services, nor could he appeal against judicial verdicts. No Christian slave could be free and churches and holy books would be destroyed; The clergy would be imprisoned and forced to sacrifice to the gods through torture. The purpose was to deprive the faithful of their leaders and the organization of the Church of its main defenders. Finally, this edict was applied to all Christians'*. The rigor with which these edicts were applied was very different in different areas of the Empire. There were some lapses - those who handed over sacred books to be destroyed were called traditors - but in numbers much smaller than those during the persecution of Decius, and there were many martyrs and confessors. It was the last battle of the Church with pagan Rome, since the battle was already close.

Simple narrative without literary pretensions, but detailed and precise, written by an eyewitness of the events he relates, it consists of three parts: a) the interrogation process before the proconsul Aspasio Paterno and the condemnation of Cúrubis to exile, on August 10, 257; b) the process of his second interrogation, before the proconsul Galerius Maximus and the death sentence, in the month of September of the year 258; and c) the account of the martyrdom, carried out on September 14 of the same year, in Villa Sexti, near Cartago 24. 3. His works constitute the main means or source that we can use to deduce the facts of his life and divine his psychological traits: his prudence, his great charity, his firmness of character. His fruitful literary production is limited to a series of pamphlets, more or less extensive treatises on apologetics, polemics or morals, and the letters he wrote while he was already a bishop. These letters do not have an indication of the date, but, thanks to their content, the year in which they were written can be deduced from almost all of them. From the first pamphlets, which probably predate all the letters, especially from the Ad Donatum, where he sings of the wonders of grace in the soul of the new Christian and the happiness with which he feels possessed by the new practices, to letter 8 1, addressed in the year 24 W. He was still a catechumen when he took a vow of continence and sold his estates to distribute the amount among the poor; He had recently been baptized when he was ordained a priest and soon, by the acclamation of all the people, he received the episcopal consecration that took him to the proconsular metropolis of Africa. We can deduce the year of his ascension to the episcopal dignity through the content of letter 59, written to Pope Cornelius in the year 252, in which he says that this is the fourth year of his pontificate. A mixture of energy - which, when he believed he was well oriented, made him intransigent in the face of anyone, no matter how high - and sweet humility - which led him to consult the opinion of his subordinates, the African bishops and the clerics and even the lay faithful - made him triumph in the not easy task of governing the first of the episcopal sees in Africa3' at a time when - as he himself says32 - the ancient discipline had been relaxed to such an extent that it was general desire to accumulate wealth, zeal and purity of faith were lacking in the ministers of God, works of mercy were not practiced, men and women disfigured the work of God in their bodies with false dyes and artifices of all kinds, they deceived one another, Christians married infidels, they swore without necessity and even falsely, they arrogantly despised the 'O

Very soon a new state of things came to make Saint Cyprian's actions even more difficult: with the ascension of Decius to the imperial throne, came the Roman reaction against foreignism, which had invaded everything with the previous foreign emperors, and a furious persecution of Christians broke out at the beginning of the year 250, when Cyprian was just a bishop. Only by fleeing could he escape death, which the Gentile people tumultuously demanded, shouting that he should be thrown to the lions of the circus 34. It was not yet time - says his biographer - for him to reach the peak of glory with martyrdom; He had to climb all the steps, one at a time, and the faithful needed his advice and help in the horrible persecution that had just broken out. The Roman clergy, in charge of the government of the Church due to the vacancy left by the martyrdom of Saint Fabian35, did not approve it as necessary for him to escape the Bishop of Carthage and write letter 20 in order to justify himself. Letter 9 and many of the later ones up to 43 also belong to this time. The persecution of ~ ecio although ~ ~, brief in time, brought as a consequence a large number of apostasies. Everyone was called to appear before the magistrates and forced to sacrifice to the gods of the official religion. Those who submitted to these conditions received a certificate of compliance and were no longer bothered. There were many Christians who did not resist. Some fell by performing a proper sacrifice - sucrificati - or offering a few grains of incense on the altar - thuriJicati, while others feigned an apostasy that did not really exist. The long peace had produced a certain laziness in many Christians, and for this reason some obtained from public employees a certificate with the testimony of having sacrificed to the gods, and others simply had themselves registered in the public lists and received the libellus in which this was recorded, for which they were called libellatici. All of them were considered by the Church as lapses or fallen, and obliged to canonical penance if they requested their reintegration into the communion of the faithful. The respect shown to the imprisoned holy confessors close to martyrdom meant that the lapses went to ask them for certificates of recommendation to the ecclesiastical authorities, with the presentation of which, called libelli pacis, they were granted the abbreviation of the penitential procedures and very often total forgiveness.

On this occasion, the Bishop of Carthage had to show all his energy, his firmness and his righteousness in order to prevent an abuse of the benevolence of the martyrs towards the lapses; To this end, Cipriano wrote letters 15, 16 and 18 from his refuge, addressed to the confessors, the clerics and the people, respectively. The bishop's orders inviting the lapses to penance and patience were not well received by everyone, since among the imprisoned confessors themselves there were those who did not want to accept them. Lucian, a man of "intrepid faith and robust virtue, but of few ~ ~, had been condemned to hunger and thirst in prison, on behalf of other imprisoned confessors addressed a brief letter to Cyprian39 in which he said: "You must know that all of us have granted peace to those who have given you an account of their conduct after the sin). The bishop remained adamant. In a letter addressed to his clerics40, he congratulates them for having excommunicated the priest Gaius of Dida, who admitted lapsed to communion, and exhorts them to act equally with anyone who follows the same conduct, whether cleric or layman. Towards the beginning of the year 25 1, the persecution subsided and Cyprian thought of returning to his church; but a new complication prevented him from doing so. In fact, the priest Novato and the layman Felicisimo, already adversaries of Saint Cyprian since, against his opinion, he had been promoted to the episcopal dignity, supported by eight other priests, raised a storm of hatred against their bishop, taking as a pretext severity, which they described as excessive.

Saint Cyprian excommunicated the insubordinate4' and returned to his metropolis towards the end of March or the beginning of April of the year 25 1, ready to resolve in a council the issue of the lapses, which had caused these unfortunate events. In preparation for this council he had written the booklet or treatise De lapsis, where he lamented the defection of so many brothers and exhorted all the fallen to penitence. It was then that the spring council of the year 25 1 met, which approved all the actions of the Bishop of Carthage. In it it is decided to receive the libellatici into ecclesial communion without prior public penance. The sacrijkati and thurijicati had to do public penance for a long time (diu). Meanwhile, another more serious schism threatened the Church. After the martyrdom of Pope Fabian, the see of Rome was vacant for fourteen months. In front of the Roman church was the presbyterium; Cornelius and Nicholas were the most influential figures within the Roman clergy. In 251 Cornelius was elected. Novatian, wounded, accused Cornelius of being lax for his kindness to the apostates and had himself consecrated by three rural bishops of Italy in haste and with deceit, having made them drunk^^^. From that moment, surrounded by a group of priests, deacons and admirers, he declared himself leader in front of Cornelius. Although it seems that the schism occurred for personal reasons rather than dogmatic or doctrinal, this counter-church continues - the Roman synod excommunicates Novatian on 25 1 - and we know Letter41. Saint Cyprian acts against this schism energetically and abundantly, first sending delegates to Rome to ascertain the facts regarding the ordination of Cornelius and that of Novatian; he writes to Cornelius telling him what is happening in Africa due to the schism46; he had Cornelius' letters read publicly4' and expelled the emissaries that Novatian had sent to Carthage4*; He then writes to the confessors of Rome who had followed Novatian and returns them to the church4'; He also wrote to Bishop Antonianus that he doubted the legality of the Bishop of Rome and the purity of his faith; He wrote again to Cornelius and the confessors of Rome and published the brief but admirable treatise De catholicae Ecclesiae unitate. Now, with all this the situation of the African Church had worsened, since at the beginning of the year 252 Novatus and his people appointed a certain Maximus bishop of Carthage and later Felicisimo's henchmen gathered four bishops deposed in previous councils and had Fortunatus, one of the greatest enemies of the legitimate bishop, Cyprian, consecrated bishop of Carthage. The biographer Pontius says nothing about all these events: from the beginning of the persecution of Decius - at the beginning of the year 250 - he moves on to the mournful days of the epidemic of 252. The havoc caused by this epidemic was terrible: the sick were abandoned by their relatives, who fled from the contagion; The dead were piled up in the middle of the street and were mercilessly looted. The Carthaginian bishop gathered the people and instructed them on the value of works of mercy and the practice of Christian charity. It was then that he published his treatises De oratione dominica, a beautiful commentary on the Lord's Prayer; De opere et eleemosynis, motivation to charity; De mortalitate, about hope in a future life; and Ad Dernetrianum, a magnificent apology for Christianity addressed to a Gentile who had echoed the public voice, which blamed the epidemic on Christians. Another sad event still gave Bishop Cyprian of Carthage the opportunity to express his generosity. A few tribes of barbarians, taking advantage of the opportunity of the 111th Augusta legion having been discharged, invaded Numidia and reduced many Christians to captivity, among whom there were some virgins consecrated to the Lord. The Numidian bishops wrote to Carthage letting him know of the misfortune, and he, immediately taking up a collection to contribute to the ransom of the captives, responded with a letter2 while sending the proceeds. Meanwhile Cyprian had become the most accredited advisor not only of the African church, to which Letter 62.

presided, but even of all the neighboring churches. And so we see that in the year 253 he wrote to Caecilius, probably bishop of Bilta, an extensive letter, in which he combated the practice, common in some African churches, of consecrating water instead of wine in the E~charist ~each~year; Next he intervenes in the matter of the Spanish bishops Basílides and Marcial54, who wanted to return to the episcopal dignity after having acquired certificates of apostasy; In the same year he wrote to the bishop of Rome, Etheban, to tell him of the excommunication of Martial, bishop of Arles, who remained a Novacianist. From the year 255 to 257 the question of the practice of rebaptizing heretics arose, to which the letters 69 to 75 refer; In the African church as well as in that of Asia Minor it was customary to rebaptize those who had received this sacrament at the hands of heretics, when they were admitted into the Catholic Church. In Rome, however, this practice was not followed, limiting itself to the laying on of hands. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, on the grounds that heretics and schismatics, not having grace, could not confer it, displayed extraordinary activity in defense of the accepted African doctrine; sent letters, answering the queries of ~ agno ' ~de, de~,~ ovino ~ and *de PompeQuinto, bishop of M a ~ ritania ~ i59; He gathered thirty-one bishops in council in the year 255, seventy-one in the year 256 and eighty-seven in the first53 Letter 63.

The bishop of Rome was inflexible and threatened African bishops with excommunication; but these remained firm, supporting the prestige of the metropolitan of Carthage and other exemplary bishops such as Firmilian of Cappadocia. No one has ever known what the end of this controversy will be. The fact is that then the persecution of Valerian began; Christians must have all united in those moments of anguish and each church must have followed its customs; At least Africa seems to have followed the practice of rebaptism until 314, at the Council of Arles, it renounced it of its own free will. The Last Letters, from 66, belong to the time of this persecution. The bishop of Carthage was summoned on August 30, 257 in the presence of the proconsul Aspasius Paterno and condemned to exile in a small coastal town called curubis6'. In this refuge Bishop Cipriano began to prepare for the martyrdom that he saw imminent; From there he wrote the treatise Ad Fortunatum, encouraging Christians to suffer persecution, and also letter 76, which he wrote to those who for their faith had been condemned to work in the mines and quarries. The Vita Cypriani and the Acta proconsularia have left a detailed relationship. The new proconsul Galerius Maximus - the Acts say - ordered that Cyprian return to Carthage, when he had been in exile for a year. The proconsul, who was then in Utica, sent for him, but he, believing that the duty of a bishop was to die among his faithful, hid and did not allow himself to be found until he learned that Galerius Maximus was in Carthage. On September 14, 258, he was taken to the proconsul's court and sentenced to be beheaded. The sentence was carried out immediately. Until the last moment, Cyprian preserved the same temper of spirit that he had maintained in his difficult duties as head of the African church in those calamitous times. 3. Literary production and style The literary style of Bishop Cyprian of Carthage is very well summarized in the praise that Lactantius gives of him: «He had, he says, an easy, abundant, soft and clear wit, and this is the best quality of a writer; It was impossible to say what stood out the most in him, the elegance of his speech, the clarity of his explanation or the strength of his persuasion))64. ~ abriolle ~ compares these words with those of Saint Jerome: «The blessed Cyprian, like a most pure fountain, advances softly and with those of Cassiodorus: it emanates like oil with all ~ gentleness))~', and he notes

how all three agree in the appreciation of this soft eloquence that expands. On the other hand, the influence that Tertullian had on him is undeniable; There are fragments in his works that seem literally inspired by the impulsive Carthaginian character. But, nevertheless, the differences between one and the other are very notable. Tertullian is vehement and aggressive to the point of often exceeding the limits of charity and even those of prudence; Cipriano, on the contrary, is measured and fair, he does not allow himself to be bowed, but in his firmness there is always a great softness; As for the language, they are also very different: Tertullian's is more expressive, richer in imagination, more original, with a more abundant lexicon and such a great property that it demonstrates a perfect mastery of the language; that of Saint Cyprian has more elegance and distinction, it is even more grammatically correct, but less brilliant. Very far from Cyprian being a servile imitator of his revered master, he has such a characteristically his own way of writing that, through it - according to Saint Augustine - the authenticity of his works can be recognized. His style is bombastic, redundant, almost always loaded with rhetorical figures; But this excessive ornamentation does not cloud the transparency of his thought in any way, it does not in any way hinder the clarity of his explanations or the force of his peruasion ~ ~. Regarding the version of the Bible used by the bishop of Carthage, it seems clear that he uses at least another Vetus different from the Vulgate. In some passages the biblical text transmitted in the quotations of Saint Cyprian contains very notable differences compared to that of the Vulgate. Many Latin versions of the Bible had to circulate in the early Western Church. The old translations, prior to the one carried out by Saint Jerome, known as the Vulgate, are called Vetus. We have documentation of them, both abundant and fragmentary, since they are known especially through biblical quotations from Latin Christian authors. Based on the studies carried out, it can be said that, at least, there was an ancient version in North Africa. Tertullian (160-220) attests to the existence of a Latin biblical text - on two occasions he refers to incorrect translations^'^ - and in the writings of Cyprian an already typified version of the Bible appears, with a fixed and uniform text, which is usually called Vetus Afra. On the other hand, different studies show that in Rome a Latin text of the Bible was used that does not coincide with the African one: for example, in the translation of the Epistle of Saint Clement Romanus, probably made in the first half of the 11th century, or in the biblical text contained in the writings of Novatian, a contemporary of Saint Cyprian. It would be the Vetus Itala. One can also speak of a Vetus Hispana, as a group of sufficiently characterized translations7'.

These primitive versions, called Vetus - that is, "old", "ancient" - are translations made on the Greek text of the Septuagint, and on good codices of the so-called Western form (or version B). As for the translation, they are characterized by being extremely literal, constantly resenting, both the constructions and the vocabulary itself, the Greek influence. This literalism has had the advantage of making the underlying Greek text easily readable, with which these Vetus have become an important element for Greek textual criticism of the Bible. As for the language, they use vulgar Latin, since the translators were concerned, above all, with making the biblical text intelligible to the people. The multiplicity of textual variants, due to continuous corrections, produced great confusion that made the need for a new and uniform translation of the Bible felt for the entire Christian West. In the year 382, Pope Saint Damasus (366-384) commissioned Saint Jerome to revise the Latin text of the Gospels: thus began the long task - first, of revising the Latin versions of Greek texts, and then, of direct translation from Hebrew to Latin - which culminated in the year 404. All this work of translating the biblical text into Latin is what is called the Vulgate Bible. The appearance of the Vulgate of Saint Jerome marked the beginning of the decline of the ancient translations, which continued, however, to be used simultaneously until the 9th century. The literary production of Saint Cyprian, as it has come down to us, consists of thirteen tracts and fifty-nine letters. Of the twenty-two letters that remain to complete the eighty-one that make up the complete epistolary, sixteen are addressed to him or related to the affairs of his

episcopal ministry and the other six are collective synods of which he was the main or perhaps the only editor. The booklets are: Quod idola dii non sint: Work from the first years of his life as a Christian, probably around 246, in which he reveals mythological errors, proves the existence of a single God and expands on considerations about the life, passion and death of Jesus Christ by whom believers are saved. The brevity, the mastery of the entire story, the brilliance of style and concept with which Cyprian proves the falsity of the idols are notorious. Testimoniorum libri tres aduersus Iudaeos: Compilation of texts from the Holy Scripture to prove to the recipient of the book, Quirinus, that the Jewish people were reproved and the Christian chosen, and to offer him a brief Christology and a safe conduct as a good Christian. It is believed to be from the year 248. Ad Donatum: Although this treatise, due to its epistolary form, could seem addressed to that specific person - we do not know who this Donatus is, since in Cyprian's epistolary we find at least five of the same name - it is rather admitted that it has a general character. Cyprian, in fact, wants to witness the wonderful change that has occurred in him through baptism and thereby encourage catechumens and pagans towards conversion. The bishop of Carthage could even have tried to distance, with his writings, the reading of Tertullian's works, which were somewhat dangerous for his readers. Now, its originality consists in the fact that Cyprian exposes his states of soul and thereby inaugurates a literary genre, in which another African, Augustine of Hippo, will be distinguished as the greatest figure in his Confessions. It corresponds to the year 249. De habitu uirginum: From the end of the same year 249. It is an exhortation against the luxury of women and

a praise of virginity. This is one of the books in which the literary influence of Tertullian is most evident, author of the works De cultu feminarum, De uelandis uirginibus and De habitu muliebri, all of which Cyprian used for this treatise. From Catholicae Ecclesiae unitate: Written to combat schism and recommend to the faithful perseverance in the unity of the Church. It is the one that has given the most name to its author, and was written in the year 25 1. Lapsis: This treatise from the same year 25 1 focuses on the problem of those who had apostatized during the persecution. De dominica oratione: From the year 252, when the epidemic that had invaded those lands made the consolation of looking up, towards the sky, so necessary. It is a treatise on prayer in general and, especially, on the Lord's Prayer. De opere et eleemosynis: From the same year 252 and for the same occasion of the plague, trying to stimulate the charity of the faithful towards those affected. De mortalitate: Also written on the occasion of the plague of 252 in order to encourage the faithful to hope and desire the true life on the other side of the tomb. Ad Demetrianum: It still deals with the plague of that year 252, which the recipient attributed to the indignation of the gods against the Christians and against those who tolerated them. The author takes the opportunity to make a very lively apology for the Christian religion. De bonus patientiae: This treatise seems to have been composed on the occasion of violent discussions that arose among the Christians of Africa, regarding the baptism of heretics. Without speaking explicitly, the bishop wants to keep his faithful in unity and charity, preaching patience, the source of unity and peace. It is from the year 256.

With Tertullian and Augustine, Cyprian has been one of the masters of thought and style in the church of Africa, and at the same time his writings are a testimony to the zeal and charity of the pastor who experienced many trials: the persecution of Decius, the division of his faithful, the attacks of heretics, the terrible plague that devastated the Roman Empire, between 252 and 254, and finally martyrdom. De zelo et liuore: Complement to the previous one and written shortly after against envy and jealousy, which are the vices that cause schisms. Ad Fortunatum: Collection of sentences extracted from the Holy Scriptures, with the intention of instilling courage in Christians in the new persecution promulgated by Valerian. This treatise is from 257. In addition, many other tracts have been attributed to our author that today everyone recognizes as spurious, among which these are notable: De laude martyrii: It is found in the anonymous catalog of 35972 where the canonical books of the Holy Scripture and the works of Saint Cyprian are collected; but his puffed-up style is evidently unbecoming of the holy bishop of Carthage. Someone attributed it to Novaciano, but it seems that it is not his either. Aduersus Iudaeos: It also appears in the catalog of 359, but it is not consistent with the Cyprian style either; It was previously considered a translation from the Greek, but this opinion was later proven to be inaccurate. This one could really be from Novaciano. De montibus Sina et Sion: By an author not yet known, but probably from the time of Saint Cyprian. 72 Discovered by Mommsen in a tenth-century manuscript from the library of Philip of Cheltenham (cf. From spectaculis: Perhaps from Novaciano. De bonus pudicitiae: Probably from the same author. Ad Nouatianum: Someone has believed it from Pope Sixtus 11, but from the content and analysis of the same text it seems to be deduced that it was written a few years before. Aduersus aleatores: Harnack took it as the work of Pope Victor 11, but it must have been later, since whoever wrote it had to know the works of Saint Cyprian and in a special way the tract Testimoniorum libri tres aduersus ludaeos. The epistolary: manuscripts and editions The Epistolary Corpus of Cyprian of Carthage, in addition to being an important source for the history of the Church and Canon Law, is an extraordinary monument of Christian Latin. Indeed, while his treatises show the influence of stylistic procedures, his letters reproduce the spoken Latin of the educated Christians of the 111th century. To find the ecclesiastical writer and the former professor of rhetoric, familiar with Cicero's phrase, we have to go to his books, where we find him with the brilliance of his style. But Cyprian's letters also constitute an inexhaustible source for the study of a very interesting period in the history of the Church, since they reflect the problems and controversies that the ecclesiastical administration had to face in the middle of the 111th century: they bring us the echo of the words of eminent personalities of the time, such as Cyprian himself, Novatian, Cornelius,

Stephen, Firmilian of Caesarea and others; They reveal to us the hopes and fears, the life and death of Christians in one of the most important provinces of Christendom at that time. The collection of letters - as we have it today - has been formed little by little. San Cipriano kept a copy of the letters he sent and attached the responses to which they referred: this way he always had at hand, so he could communicate to whoever it was, what he had written to others. On several occasions he himself says in his letters that he attached others to them, either his own or ones he had received. Along with letter 20, he sent to the clergy of Rome, in order to justify his flight, copies of thirteen letters that he had addressed to the clerics of Carthage, to the confessors, to the exiles and to all the faithful; With the 25th he sent five to Caldonio explaining his actions in the matter of the lapses; Together with the 32nd he sent to the clerics of Carthage copies of the letters addressed by him to the clerics and confessors of Rome and of the responses they had made to him. In this way he himself began to form small partial collections of letters referring to the same topic73. After his death, his disciples expanded these collections and used them for the edification and instruction of the faithful74. Of the eighty-one pieces that comprise the Epistolary Corpus in modern editions, sixteen were written to Cyprian or the clergy of Carthage: this last group contains letters from the clergy of Rome, from Novatian, from Bishop Cornelius of Rome and others. The year of writing this letter is not recorded, and that is why there is a lot of variety in its order of placement within the different epistolaries. We follow that of Canon Bayard, who is the same as Hartel. The word presbyter has a rather technical character, and predominates as a position within the ecclesial administration. Cyprian uses it to designate the priest, since the word sacerdos is often used with the meaning of bishop. Later, in note to letter 3, we refer to priests. "Deacon" is a Greek word; In Hellenistic times and in epigraphy it has the meaning of "servant of a temple", and that is the meaning of deacon, in the Latin of the Church, which has been preserved to this day. After Christ ascended to heaven, the apostles created this ministry, as reported in the Acts of the Apostles, 6, 1-7: the diaconate is, therefore, in the Church a sacred ministry of apostolic origin. The 11th Vatican Council states, confirming the reality transmitted from age to age, that deacons serve the people of God in the ministry of the liturgy, the word and charity. (Cf. CONST., Lumen Gentium 29.) Fumi was a town, episcopal seat, of Tunisia, within the Medjerda valley, of which mention is made in the Carthaginian council of the year 256.

It deeply affected me and my colleagues who were present, very dear brothers, and all our priests who advised us, to know that our brother Geminius Victor had made, at the hour of his death, a will in which he named the priest Geminius 'Austinus' as guardian, being as it has been decreed for some time in an episcopal council16 that no one name in his will any guardian or curator. clergyman or minister of God, since those who have received the honor of the divine priesthood and have been constituted members of the clergy, must only serve the altar and the sacrifices, and must attend to their prayers and prayers. For it is written: "A soldier of God does not engage in secular affairs if he wants to please the one who has taken him into his service." And if this has been said of everyone in general, how much more reason should those who, being consecrated to the things of God and the spirit, cannot distance themselves from the Church to occupy themselves with earthly and secular matters not involve themselves in the annoying concerns and obstructions of the things of the world? The Levites of the old law had this discipline and this religion, so that, eleven tribes dividing the land and dividing its possession, that of Levi, dedicated to the service of the temple, the altar and the divine ministries, did not receive anything from that distribution, but was concerned only with the worship of God while the rest were dedicated to the cultivation of the land, and received from the other eleven for their subsistence the tithe of the fruits that the land produced.

This was done then by order of God himself, so that those who were engaged in divine works would not be distracted by anything else or be forced to think or get involved in secular business. Today the same discipline applies to the clerics: those who in the Church of the Lord are promoted to clerical ordination, must not be diverted under any circumstances from the administration of divine things, so that they do not feel attracted by the annoying cares and business of the century, but, receiving with honor part of the food that their brothers offer them in replacement of the old tithes, they do not turn away from the altar or the sacrifices and live day and night busy. in the things of heaven and the spirit. Scrupulously keeping this in mind and showing a healthy providence, our predecessor bishops determined to order that no dying faithful appoint a clergyman as tutor or curator and that, if someone did so, no suffrages would be offered for him or the sacrifice celebrated for his repose. For he who wanted the priests and ministers to distance themselves from the altar does not deserve to be named before the altar of God in the prayer of the priests. Brother: this word, in the New Testament, specifically designates those who have the same faith: it is, therefore, the name that the Christians of the early Church gave to each other. In the fraternal community of the early Church, this expression is based on Jesus as brother and as the new Adam, and on the new message of Jesus, love appearing as a fundamental attitude of this fraternal community, which unites all Christians among themselves; The presupposition of Christian fraternal love is the common rebirth through faith in the Lord and in his redeeming love. In the Acts of the Apostles, the apostolic letters and the Apocalypse, the general designation of brothers is applied to all Christians. Cyprian to the priests and deacons Cyprian, in hiding due to the persecution of the edict of Decius at the end of 249, worries about his faithful and asks the clergy to care for the imprisoned confessors - with caution when visiting prisons - and the poor.

Cipriano greets the priests and deacons, his very dear brothers. I am well by the grace of God, dear brothers, 1 and I convey my greetings to you, very happy knowing that your health is also good. And since the circumstances

locals do not allow me to be with you now, I ask you, for your faith and your religiosity, to do so for you and for me, so that nothing is lacking in discipline or diligence. As for the distribution of the money, both to those who are in prison for having gloriously confessed the Lord, and to those who persevere constantly in the Lord despite their poverty and indigence, I pray that they do not lack anything, since the small amount that was collected was distributed there among the clerics for cases like this, so that more would have something to draw from to meet their particular needs and difficulties. I also ask you to put your skill and your careful care into play to ensure calm. For as much as the brothers, moved by love, feel eager to meet and visit the good confessors whom divine goodness has already made illustrious with glorious beginnings, I understand that this must be done with caution and not in agglomeration or gathering at the same time in a large crowd, to avoid that this itself provokes aversion and denial of permission to enter, and that by insatiably seeking too many things, we lose everything. Take heed, then, and provide so that by wise moderation this may be done in a safer manner, so that even the presbyters who come there to officiate the sacrifice before the confessors, go one by one with a different deacon each time, because the change of persons and the variety of visitors lessens hatred. We must be sweet and humble in all things as befits servants of God and, adjusting to current circumstances, seek peace and care for the people. I wish, dearest and much missed brothers, that you always enjoy good health and remember me. Greet the entire community of brothers. The deacon greets you and also everyone who is with me. Bye bye.

Cyprian to Sergius and Rogatian and other confessors Cyprian strongly exhorts the confessors regrouped with Sergius and Rogatian, through the highest motives of faith, encouraging them to perseverance and to be faithful in the confession of the Lord.

Cyprian to Sergius and ~ ogacian oy ~ to ~ all, the other confessors 35, wishes you perpetual health in God. I greet you, dear brothers, also wishing to enjoy your presence, if the situation of the place where I am would allow me to approach you36. Because what could be more desirable and more pleasant for me than to find myself now among you so that you could embrace me with those hands that, pure and innocent and faithful to the Lord, rejected sacrilegious offerings?; what else 34 This Rogatian is the same one mentioned in the following letter and the recipient of letters 13 and 41. 35 Confessors and martyrs: the Greek word martys, originally, had the meaning of a witness of faith, not necessarily that of suffering martyrdom. In Saint Hippolytus and Tertullian, martyrs are those who succumb, while those who survive are confessors. Cyprian to the priests and deacons Cyprian, who is eager to return to his Church but fears provoking the pagans with his presence, once again expresses his concern for his flock, remembering the help of widows, the sick and all those in need: through the acolyte Naricus he sends money to Rogatianus.
Cipriano greets the priests and deacons, very dear brothers. i

I greet you, dear brothers; I am well by the grace of God and I long to go to you immediately, to satisfy my desire, which is yours and that of all the brothers. It is necessary, however, that we look after the common peace and that, despite the feeling of our hearts, we temporarily remain absent from you, so that our presence does not provoke the hatred and violence of the Gentiles and that we are responsible for the rupture of the peace, precisely those who must seek the tranquility of all. Therefore, when you write to me that everything is now settled and I can return, or if the Lord deigns to tell me before, then I will join you. Well, where could I find myself better and happier than where God wanted me to be?

For you are not ignorant of the serious danger that exists, if you do not exhort our brothers to remain unshakable in the faith, lest, by falling into idolatry, the community of brothers be profoundly destroyed. And we do not exhort you to this only with words, but you will be able to be informed by the many who are coming to you from here; because with the help of God we have done and continue to practice such things with the greatest care, even exposing ourselves to the material dangers of the century, setting our eyes more on the fear of God and eternal punishments than on the fear of men and temporary abuses, without abandoning our brothers, and encouraging them to remain constant in the faith and to be ready, as is their duty, to go with the Lord. But we have even made those who ascended to do something they were forced to do57. The Church remains standing, firm in the faith, despite the fact that some, overcome with terror, either because they were people of position, or because when they were arrested they gave in due to human weakness, they have fallen: these, certainly, even separated from us, we have not abandoned, but we have exhorted them and continue to exhort them to do penance, in case they can obtain forgiveness from Him who can grant it, lest, if we abandon them, they become worse. Therefore, you see, brothers, that you also 3 must do this, so that those who have fallen, repentant thanks to your exhortations, if they are arrested again, may confess and so that they can repair their past error; Other things also concern you, which we also remind you here: if those who fell in the persecution were attacked by the en-

Cyprian to the priests and deacons of Rome Cyprian, aware of the death of Pope Fabian, dedicates glowing words to him. Regarding the previous letter, which arrived without a signature or clear recipient, return the original so that its legitimacy can be confirmed.

Cyprian greets the brother priests and deacons of Rome. Having reached me, dear brothers, the uncertain rumor of the death of my colleague6', good man, and, being in doubt, I received from you the letter that you sent me by the subdeacon Crementius; Through her I was informed in every detail of his glorious death, and I had great joy because the integrity of his administration had also received such an honorable coronation. In this regard, I also sincerely congratulate you because you praise his memory with such a general and splendid testimony, allowing us to know through you what for you, remembering your Bishop, is a great glory, and also offers us an example of faith and virtue. For just as the fall of a leader perniciously influences the fall of those who follow him, in the same way, on the contrary, the firmness in faith, by which the bishop lends himself to being imitated by his brothers, is beneficial and healthy.
It refers to Pope Saint Fabihn, who died a martyr on January 20, 250.

I have also read another letter, which does not explicitly indicate who wrote it or to whom it is addressed. And since the way of writing and the meaning and even the material support of the letter have made me fear that something about the truth has been suppressed or changed, I have sent you the same original letter, so that you can recognize if it is the same one that you gave to subdeacon Crementius 2 to bring. It would indeed be very serious if the true text of a letter from the clergy were altered by fraud or deception. Examine, then, so that we can know, whether the writing and signature is yours, and write to us what is true. I wish, dear brothers, that you are always well.

confessors of Christ. But the current confession is all the more glorious and honorable the stronger the tribulation: the combat has intensified, the glory of the combatants has also been magnified. And you have not left the light? It was because of fear of the torments, but because of the same reasons you felt more impelled to the fighting field, and strong and courageous, you returned to the fight with brave courage for the greatest of tests. 2 I have learned that some of you have already been crowned, that some, likewise, are close to the crown of victory, and that all, in short, those who, forming a glorious squadron, suffered the straitness of prison, are animated by the heat of the same courage to fight the combat as the soldiers of Christ must be in the divine camp, so that neither flattery seduces the unbreakable firmness of faith, nor do they Let them not be frightened by threats, nor overcome by punishments and torments, because he who is within us is greater than he who is in this world, and he has no greater strength to abate earthly punishment than divine protection to revive. The facts have been demonstrated in the glorious combat of the brothers; They, converted into guides for others in the art of overcoming torment, gave an example of bravery and fidelity, fighting in combat until the enemy succumbed, defeated. Therefore, with what praise will I praise you, 2 most brave brothers? With what eloquent words will I extol the strength of your feelings and the perseverance of your faith? You have tolerated the harshest torture until you reached the apex of glory, and you did not bow down to the tortures, but rather the torments gave way before you. The crowns of victory provided an end to your sufferings that the instruments of torture did not provide. More cruel carnage continued, not to stop

Cyprian to the martyrs and confessors Cyprian extols the courage and perseverance of Mapálicus and a group of his colleagues armed, as soldiers of Christ, with the weapons of faith in the torments of the persecution of Decius.
Cyprian wishes the martyrs and confessors of Jesus Christ, our Lord, eternal health in God the Father 62. I

I exult with joy, most courageous and very happy brothers, and I congratulate you once you know your fidelity and courage, of which Mother Church glories, she who recently, certainly, was also proud of the pain that, due to your persistent confession, turned 62 into exiles. This letter is a clear example of the literary training of Cyprian, a disciple in love with the literature of his teacher Tertullian.

to pray for constant fidelity, but to send the men of God more quickly to the Lord. The multitude of those present could see, surprised, the heavenly test for God and the spiritual combat for Christ; how his servants maintained themselves with free expression, with incorruptible spirit, with superhuman courage; certainly devoid of weapons of this world, but armed with those of faith. They showed themselves strong in the torments, stronger than those who tormented them, and their beaten and destroyed limbs defeated the hooks that hit and tore them. The cruel wound, opened again and again, could not overcome the impregnable faith, even when, the entrails torn, not only the members were tortured, but the very wounds of the servants of God. The blood flowed to extinguish the fire of persecution, to drown in its glorious current the flames and fires of hell. Oh, how worthy of the Lord was that spectacle, how sublime, how great, how pleasing in the eyes of God for the fidelity and devotion of his soldiers, as it is written in the Psalms, by the voice of the Holy Spirit, who at the same time warns us: ((Precious is the death of his righteous in the eyes of God))! 63. This death is precious, which bought immortality at the price of one's own blood, which received the crown at the cost of the consummation of its value. How joyful Christ was there, how gladly he fought and conquered in these servants of his, protecting their faith, and giving to believers as much as the one who receives believes he receives! He was present in that combat in his honor; He encouraged, sustained and strengthened those who fought and glorified his name. And he who once conquered death for us always emerges triumphant in us. «When they hand you over - he says, don't think what you are going to say. I'm afraid it's not you who

"You speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you" 64. The present combat has given us a testimony of the 4 facts. A voice filled with the Holy Spirit burst forth from the lips of the martyr, when the blessed Mapálico said to the proconsul1 in the midst of his torments: ((Tomorrow you will witness the fight)). And the Lord fulfilled what he said in testimony of his courage and his faith. The heavenly test was celebrated and in the contest of the promised combat the servant of God was crowned. The prophet Isaiah was referring to this test when he said: 2 "It is not a petty quarrel between you and men, for God directs the battle." It is the test of our faith, for which we fight, for which we conquer and for which we are crowned. This is the test that the apostle Saint Paul also showed us 3, in which it is appropriate for us to run and reach the glory of the crown. «Don't you know, he says, that the competitors in the stadium all run, but only one receives the palm? Run so that you get it. And those, by the way, to receive a perishable palm, but we incorruptible))67. libation and the time of departure approaches. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my race, I have kept the faith. All I need now is the crown of justice that the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day; but not only to me, but to all those who desired his coming."68 In fact, Mapálico, in his own name and in that of his colleagues, committed himself again before the proconsul to this combat, previously predicted by the prophets, entrusted by the Lord, carried out by the apostles. And the faithful word did not fail in its promise: it fought the combat that it promised, and received the palm 4 that it deserved. I wish - and I urge you - that you too follow this martyr, now blessed, and the others who participated in the same combat and were his companions in the firmness of faith, patient in pain, victorious in torture: so that those who were united by the bond of confession and the hospitality of prison, may also be united by the consummation of courage and the heavenly crown; and with your joy you wipe away the tears of Mother Church, which mourns the fall and death of so many, and encourage the perseverance of others, who also remain firm with the encouragement of your example. If combat calls you, if the day of your trial comes to you, be brave soldiers, fight without fainting, knowing that you fight under the gaze of the Lord whom you keep in mind, that by confessing his name you reach his glory, and that he is not content with observing his servants, but he himself fights among us, he himself fights, he himself, at the end of our combat, gives the crown and is crowned. But if, by the mercy of the Lord, peace comes before the day of your combat, nevertheless a complete will and a glorious conscience remain in you. and

Let no one of you be saddened as inferior to those who, having endured the torments before you, and after trampling and conquering the world, by a triumphant path came to the presence of the Lord. The Lord searches the depths of the heart, penetrates the secrets and sees the hidden. To deserve the crown at His hands the sole testimony of Him, who is the one who will judge us, is enough. Both facts are, therefore, 2 very dear brothers, at the same time sublime and illustrious: the one, safer, going quickly before the Lord, once the victory is consummated; the other, more joyful, having obtained liberation through the glory of martyrdom, flourishes in the esteem of the Church. Oh blessed Church of ours, which is thus illuminated by the splendor of divine goodness, which is given luster in our times by the glorious blood of the martyrs! Before, she appeared white in the brothers' works; now it has become purple with the blood of the martyrs. There is no shortage of lilies or roses among its flowers. Let each one fight now to obtain the highest dignity of both honors. May he receive his crown, now white for his works, now red for his martyrdom. In the camp of heaven, not only peace but also struggle have their flowers, with which the soldier of Christ is crowned for his triumph. I wish, most courageous and very happy brothers, that you always remain well in the Lord and that you remember me. Bye bye.

torments, and torments in which the executioner has no end, nor condemnation promulgated, nor death a consolation; torments that do not easily lead to receiving the crown, but rather torment until they apostatize, unless someone takes advantage of having been delivered by divine goodness at the very moment of the torment, achieving glory not because the torment has been put to an end, but because death came quickly. We suffer all this deservedly because of ourselves, 2 just as the divine warning warned us, saying: "If you forsake my law, and do not walk according to my judgments, if you profane my precepts and do not keep my commandments, I will punish your iniquities with the rod and your crimes with stripes)70. Therefore, we feel the rods and the whips since we do not please God with good works or satisfy Him for sins. Let us implore God's mercy from the depths of our hearts and with our whole soul, because he also added, saying: "But I will not turn my mercy away from them." Let us ask and we will receive, and if there is delay and delay in receiving, because we have seriously offended him, let us knock, for it opens to whoever knocks72, as long as those who knock at the door are our prayers, our groans and tears, in which it is advisable to insist and maintain, and as long as the prayer is unanimous. Now, what has most encouraged me and moved me to address this letter, you must know that it has been, just as the Lord deigns to manifest and reveal, that it was said in a vision: "Ask and you will obtain"); that then the people present were ordered to ask for some specific people, but when they asked the voices were dissonant and the wills were disparate,

Cipriano greets the brother priests and deacons. Although I know, dear brothers, that because of the fear that we all owe to God, you also engage in assiduous prayers and insistent prayers, yet I urge your religious concern to appease God and beseech him by lamenting not only in words, but also with fasting, with tears and with all kinds of insistent prayers. Because we must understand and admit that a tribulation as devastating as this persecution, which has devastated most of our flock and continues to ravage it, has been a consequence of our sins, because we did not follow the ways of the Lord or fulfill the heavenly precepts that have been given to us for our salvation. Our Lord fulfilled the will of the Father, and we do not fulfill the will of God, since we give ourselves over to the profit of temporal goods, we harbor feelings of pride, we entertain ourselves in rivalries and dissensions; we neglect simplicity and fidelity, we renounce the world in word only, but not in deed; We are each lenient with ourselves and severe with everyone else. And so we are beaten, as we deserve, as it is written: "But the servant who knows the will of his master and does not obey it, will be severely beaten." In fact, what spankings do we not deserve, when not even the confessors, who should set an example of good morals to others, maintain discipline? Therefore, while some are insolently arrogant by the inflated and shameless boasting of their confession, the i

and that the one who had said "ask and you shall obtain" was greatly displeased by the fact that the inconstant people disagreed and there was no simple and intimate union and concord among the brothers, when it is written: "God who makes those who are in harmony live in the same house^^^, and it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: "The multitude of believers acted with one spirit and heart))74; and the Lord recommended with his own word: "This is my command, that you love one another"75, and again: "I say to you that if there is agreement between two of you on earth, regarding anything you ask, it will be granted to you by my Father, who is in heaven."76 If, then, two united in spirit can do so much, what would it be if unanimity were in all. Therefore, if in accordance with the peace that the Lord gave us, all the brothers agreed, we would have long ago obtained what we asked for from divine mercy, and we would not fluctuate for a long time in this danger of our salvation and our faith; In fact, these evils would not have come upon our brothers if only one spirit had animated them all. Now, it has also been shown that a father of a family sat down with a somewhat sad young man sitting on his right, with concern and a certain indignation; he sat in his seat with his hand on his cheek and with sadness painted on his face. Another in turn, standing on the left side, carried a net, and threatened to throw it in order to capture the surrounding people. And, as the one who saw it wondered in wonder what this could mean, he was told that the young man who remained like this on the right, was saddened and hurt because-

that its precepts were not observed; which, on the contrary, the one on the left disfmted, because he was given the opportunity to obtain permission from the father of the family to be cruel. This manifested itself long before this devastating storm broke out. And we see fulfilled what had been shown, so that, while we despise the precepts of the Lord, while we do not fulfill the salutary prescriptions of the law that was given to us, the enemy has obtained permission to do harm, to cast the net and catch in it those least armed and least prepared to repel him. Let us pray insistently and groan in the midst of continuous prayers. Well, you must also know, dear brothers, that not long ago we were reproved in vision that we fell asleep in our prayers, and did not pray attentively. And, certainly, God, who loves those who rebuke, when he rebukes he does so to correct and he corrects to save. So, let us wake up and break the bonds of sleep, and pray insistently and attentively, as the apostle Paul prescribes, when he says: "Insist in prayer and with a vigilant spirit." The apostles, in fact, did not stop praying day and night, and the Lord himself, our teacher in doctrine and guide for us and example, prayed frequently and diligently, as we read in the gospel: "He went out on the mountain to pray and was in prayer with God during the night."78 And, really, what he asked for in prayer, he asked for us, since he was not a sinner, but he bore our sins. And he prayed for our sins in such a way that we read in another place:

let your faith fail»79. Therefore, if he suffers, watches and begs for us and for our crimes, how much more must we insist with prayers, and pray, first of all begging the Lord himself, and then satisfying God the Father through his 3 mediation! We have an advocate and intercessor for our sins in Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, provided we repent of our past sins and, now recognizing and confessing that we have offended the Lord with our sins, promise to walk in His ways in the future and respect His precepts. Our Father corrects us and protects us if we remain firm in the faith, and tenaciously adhere to Christ even in the midst of tribulations and persecutions, as it is written: «Who can separate us from the love of Christ: tribulation, anguish, persecution, famine, poverty, dangers, the sword?))O'. None of all this can separate believers, nothing can tear apart those who are united to his body and blood. The present persecution is a test and a probe of our disposition. God wanted us to be shaken and tested, in the same way that he has always tested his own, but in his trials he has never lacked help for believers. Finally he, out of his kindness towards us, deigned to commend me, the last of his servants, although burdened with abundant sins and unworthy of his consideration: ((Tell him, he said, to be calm, because peace is to come, but there is still a small delay, because there are still 2 some to try)). But we are also admonished by divine goodness about frugality in eating and sobriety in drinking, so that the heart, already elevated with great celestial vigor, may not be enervated by the spells of the

world, or the mind, dulled by abundance of food, becomes less fit to watch in prayer. I should not have hidden or kept for myself alone any of these visions, with which each of us can not only educate ourselves but also govern ourselves. In short, do not keep this letter hidden from yourselves, but rather advise the brothers to read it. For to intercept what the Lord deigns to warn and instruct us with is not wanting your brother to be instructed and admonished. May they know that we are being tested by our Lord, 2 and may they not be discouraged by the violence of the present tribulation in the faith by which we once believed in him. Each one recognizing his sins, immediately ((leave the works of the old man))". It is enough for us to beg forgiveness from the Lord with simplicity and unanimity, without ceasing in supplications and with the faith of achieving what we ask for, begging with lamentations and tears, as begs those who are placed between the fallen who lament and the rest of those who fear falling, between the multitude of sick people lying on the ground and the very few who remain standing. Let us ask that peace be returned to us quickly, that we may soon be helped in our hiding places and dangers, that what the Lord deigns to announce to his servants may be fulfilled: the reestablishment of his Church, the assurance that we are safe, the serenity after the storm, the light after the darkness, the sweet calm after storms and hurricanes, the compassionate help of his fatherly love, the well-known wonders of divine power; with all of which the blasphemy of the persecutors is refuted, the penance of the fallen is restored and the firm and immutable fidelity of the persevering is glorified. Cipriano greets the brother priests and deacons.

Cyprian to the priests and deacons He cares about those who die gloriously in prison; without being tormented, their value and glory are not at all inconsiderable; They can be considered among the blessed martyrs: that is why he warns Tertullus to write down the day on which they die.

Although I know, dear brothers, that you have been frequently warned in my letters to take full care of those who have confessed with a glorious voice to the Lord and are imprisoned, nevertheless, once again I charge you that nothing be lacking in concern for those who lack nothing in glory. And I wish that the condition of my position and dignities4 would allow me to be able to be personally present now: promptly and willingly in an ordinary service, I would fulfill all the duties of charity towards our brave brothers. But may your zeal fulfill my duty and do all that is necessary for those whom divine grace has exalted with such merits of fidelity and courage. There is also great interest and great care in the bodies of all those who, despite not having been tortured, end up in prison with a glorious death. For neither their value nor their glory are so small that they too cannot be included among the blessed martyrs. As for them, they suffered everything they were willing and determined to suffer. Whoever, under the gaze of God, offered himself to torment and death, suffered whatever he agreed to suffer in his will. Because it was not he himself who failed the torments, but the torments that failed him. «3 Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess before me says the Lord; they have confessed. «He who endures to the end, he will be saved))86, adds the Lord; They resisted and preserved the merits of their virtues intact and immaculate to the end. And this 84 HIS episcopal dignity, known to the Gentiles, had further irritated their hatred against the Christians.

also written: "Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life"87: they persevered faithful until death, constant and invincible. When death in prison and in chains is added to our desire and our confession, the glory of martyrdom has been consummated. Finally, also write down the days on which they die, so that we can celebrate their commemoration among the martyrs; although Tertullus, our most faithful and devout brother, in the midst of his occupations, with the zeal and care that he puts into all kinds of services to his brothers and that is not lacking even in what concerns the bodies, has written to me and continues to write to me pointing out the days in which, being in prison, our blessed brothers leave this world with glorious death towards eternity; and that we also celebrate oblations and sacrifices here in their commemoration, which very soon, with the help of God, we will celebrate in your company. May your diligent zeal not fail the poor either, as I have already written several times; to those, it is understood, who, being constant in the faith and fighting at our side with courage, have not abandoned the camp of Christ. To these, certainly, in such circumstances, we must give greater signs of affection and attention, since, neither depressed by poverty nor demolished by the force of persecution, faithfully serving the Lord, they have given an example of fidelity to the remaining poor. I wish you, dearest and most prayed brothers, that you remain in good health and remember me. Greet the brothers in my name. Goodbye8.

Cyprian to the priest Rogatian and the others The fundamental objective of this letter, a magnificent historical testimony of early Christianity, is to severely admonish those who abandon the practice of Christian truths, whether in word or deed.

Cipriano greets the priest Rogaciano and the other brother confessors. Some time ago, dear and very brave brothers, I addressed you a letter to congratulate you with encouraging words for your faith and virtue, and now my words have no other capital purpose than to joyfully proclaim once again and without ceasing the glory of your name. Because, can I wish for anything greater or better than to see the flock of Christ illuminated with the beauty of your confession? For if all the brothers are to rejoice in this, a greater share of the common joy belongs to the bishop, since the honor of the Church is the honor of its leader. As much as we grieve for those whom the disastrous storm overthrew, we rejoice just as much for you, whom the devil could not overthrow. We exhort you, therefore, by our common faith, by the sincere and pure love of our hearts towards you, that you, who have defeated the enemy in the first combat, preserve your glory with firm and persevering courage. We are still in the world, still on the battlefield.
This letter is the one mentioned in letters 13.7 and 14.2.

Also Victor, who has gone from reader to deacon and is at my side, has sent you one hundred and seventy-five. I am moved when I know that many of our brothers, spurred by charity, go to each other and alleviate your needs with their contributions. I wish, dear brother, that you are always in good health.

Cyprian to the priests and deacons Cyprian is aware of the loss that the persecution has caused the people, which has also decimated a part of the clergy, and believes it is preferable to remain hidden. He asks for their help to assist the confessors of the faith. Cipriano greets his brother priests and deacons. I wished, dear brothers, to be able to greet all our clergy intact and safe with my letter. But since the adverse storm, which has devastated most of our people, also added, to top off our pain, that with its ravages even a part of the clergy was decimated, we pray to the Lord that, knowing that you remain firm in faith and virtue, we can greet you by seeing you so constant from now on thanks to divine mercy. And, although there was a reason that impelled me, as if it were a duty, to join you soon myself, firstly the desire and desire to see you - this desire is of the greatest importance for me -, secondly to be able to discuss in common those matters regarding the government of the Church that the common good requires and, once these have been examined with the opinion of many, regulate them; However, it has seemed preferable to me to remain hidden and quiet for some time with a view to other conveniences that affect the peace and well-being of all of us, which our dearest brother Tertullus 'O' will explain to you. He, with the great care he takes i
